name: San people
info: The San are the Indigenous hunter-gatherer peoples of southern Africa, whose cultures are the oldest surviving in the region; they endured dispossession and mass killing under colonial rule, and most live today in Botswana and Namibia.

facts.homeland: Southern Africa: recent ancestral territories across Botswana, Namibia, Angola, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Lesotho and South Africa, many communities in the Kalahari; about 63,500 San in Botswana (2017) and 71,201 in Namibia (2023); places include the Tsodilo Hills, Nyae Nyae, Ghanzi and the Central Kalahari Game Reserve.
facts.period: Hunter-gatherer groups spread from Tanzania to Cape Agulhas some 10,000 years ago; the Tshua and Khwe San in the first millennium BCE; most San leave the coasts after the Khoe and Xhosa migrations from 650 CE; Dutch settlement at the Cape from 1652 and frontier killings through the 18th century; government farming programmes from the 1950s to the 1990s.
facts.known: hunting with bows and poisoned arrows and long tracking; gathering by women; sip wells and ostrich-egg water containers; rock paintings across southern Africa; rainmaking and trance; a gift economy and decisions by consensus; languages with click consonants; some of the earliest-branching human genetic lineages
facts.sources: San oral tradition and mythology, recorded by Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd (Specimens of Bushman Folklore, 1911) and Dorothea Bleek; Dutch East India Company and colonial records; archaeology such as Border Cave; the ethnography and films of Lorna Marshall, John Marshall and Elizabeth Marshall Thomas; rock-art studies by David Lewis-Williams; Y-chromosome, mitochondrial and whole-genome studies; San councils and organisations today.

t: The San, who call themselves by the names of their own nations such as the ǃKung, ǀXam and Khwe, descend from hunter-gatherer societies that some 10,000 years ago were spread from Tanzania to Cape Agulhas.
Traditionally semi-nomadic and egalitarian, they lived by hunting and gathering, took decisions by consensus with women as relative equals, and shared through a gift economy.

From the 18th century Dutch colonists’ commandos killed thousands of San at the Cape, and in 1777 the Dutch East India Company endorsed a policy of eradicating them; in Botswana the San have since been moved off land such as the Central Kalahari Game Reserve.
dyk: In long droughts the San dig into damp sand and suck water up through a hollow grass stem, letting it run down a second straw into an empty ostrich egg.
ev: As the Khoe and Xhosa move into the Eastern Cape, most San leave the coasts for the interior
The Dutch settle at the Cape of Good Hope, where the Cape San number an estimated 30,000 to 50,000
The Dutch East India Company’s loan farm system sends Trekboer stock farmers into San lands
The Dutch East India Company officially endorses a policy of eradicating the San
Louis Anthing estimates that no more than 500 San are left in all of Bushmanland, facing starvation
The worst genocidal violence against the San in German South West Africa falls in the area from Otavi to Gobabis
The San win a benefit-sharing agreement over their knowledge of the hoodia plant, and their representatives ask to be called by their own nations’ names

sections.origins:
The San are the Indigenous hunter-gatherer peoples of southern Africa. They have no collective word for themselves: they use the names of their own nations, such as the ǃKung (including the Juǀʼhoansi), ǀXam, Nǁnǂe, Khwe, Haiǁom, Gǁana and Gǀui, and in 2003 their representatives asked that these names be used where possible. “San” comes from a derogatory Khoekhoe word for foragers without cattle, and “Bushmen”, from the 17th-century Dutch Bosjesmans, is considered pejorative by many, though some San use it of themselves. In Botswana they are called Basarwa. Their languages belong to the Khoe, Tuu and Kxʼa families and have click consonants.

There is a general consensus that the modern San descend from the oldest societies of southern and eastern Africa. Some 10,000 years ago such groups were spread from Tanzania, Zambia and Angola down to Cape Agulhas, and in the first millennium BCE, by Mellet’s account, the Tshua San held the Shashe-Limpopo basin while the Khwe San lived further west. Tools almost identical to those of modern San, found at Border Cave in KwaZulu-Natal, date to 42,000 BCE.

Genetics shows great depth. The San carry some of the earliest-branching Y-chromosome and mitochondrial lineages, among them haplogroup L0d, and the ǂKhomani San are among the most genetically diverse living humans. Estimates of when their ancestors diverged from other people differ: about 200,000 years ago in a 2016 study, 360,000 to 260,000 years ago in a 2017 study of three 2,000-year-old genomes from KwaZulu-Natal.
sections.society:
The San were traditionally semi-nomadic, moving with the seasons within defined areas according to water, game and edible plants. Camps ranged from nightly rain shelters in spring, when people moved constantly in search of budding greens, to formal rings around permanent waterholes in the dry season; early spring, hot and dry, was the hardest time. Women gathered fruit, berries, tubers and bush onions, carrying food, firewood and babies in a hide cloak called a kaross and digging with a stick, and insects gave perhaps a tenth of the animal protein eaten. Men, and sometimes women, hunted on long tracking trips with bows, arrows and spears tipped with diamphotoxin, a slow-acting poison from the larvae of Diamphidia beetles.

Society was traditionally egalitarian. Where there were hereditary chiefs their authority was limited, and decisions were taken by consensus, with women treated as relative equals; women could lead family groups and claim ownership of water holes and foraging areas. The economy was a gift economy, built on regular giving rather than trade. Children had no duties besides play, and people of all ages spent much time in conversation, joking, music and dance.

Kinship follows a name rule and an age rule: the older of two people decides what to call the younger. About 35 names circulate for each sex, and a child is named after a grandparent or another relative, never a parent.
sections.beliefs:
Neighbouring peoples held that the San had a closer bond with the old spirits of the land and often turned to them for rainmaking, as at Mapungubwe. San shamans entered a trance and went into the spirit world themselves to capture the animals associated with rain. On this ground Mellet argues that the San took part in the early foundations of the Kingdom of Mapungubwe and of the states that followed it, such as Great Zimbabwe and the Mutapa Empire. Sacred dances remain part of San life.

San religion has been linked to very old practice: a find interpreted in 2006 as perhaps the world’s oldest ritual has been taken as evidence that San culture is the oldest still practised. Their stories and mythology were recorded by Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd in Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911) and by Dorothea Bleek in Mantis and His Friend. One San belief holds that a solar eclipse happens when a crocodile eats the sun.

David Lewis-Williams has studied the symbolic meanings of southern San rock paintings and drawn parallels between them and prehistoric art around the world. Outsiders have often romanticised San belief: Laurens van der Post called the Bleek collections “a sort of Stone Age Bible”, and his critics said that his books cast the San as “children of Nature” or “mystical ecologists”.
sections.arts:
Early San societies left a rich legacy of paintings on rock across southern Africa, showing hunting, battles, domestic life and mythological events. A BBC series of 2005 set San paintings made about 200 years ago beside Palaeolithic European paintings 14,000 years old, drawing on David Lewis-Williams’s work on their symbolic meanings, and Richard Wicksteed’s film In God’s Places (1995) follows the San cultural legacy of the southern Drakensberg. The Tsodilo Hills of northern Botswana bear particular witness to the long presence of the San there.

San crafts serve a life on the move: the kaross cloak, the hide sling and smaller bags, the digging stick, ostrich eggshells used as water containers, and bows, arrows and spears for the hunt, with the poison that comes from beetle larvae. Music, sacred dance and storytelling fill much of the time of people of every age, and San languages, rich in click consonants, carry a large body of stories and myths.

The San have also been filmed and written about for more than half a century. John Marshall documented the Juǀʼhoansi of Nyae Nyae from 1951 to 2000, and his sister Elizabeth Marshall Thomas wrote The Harmless People (1959). Jamie Uys’s comedy The Gods Must Be Crazy was made when the ǃKung had recently been forced into sedentary villages, and its San actors were confused by instructions to act out exaggerated versions of a hunting life they had almost abandoned.
sections.exchange:
As herders and farmers moved south, the San met them. Both the Tshua and the Khwe San dealt with migrant herders, who later became the Khoekhoe, and with herder-farmers of the Bantu expansion (2000 BCE–1000 CE), and were partly driven from their ancestral lands or absorbed into Bantu-speaking groups. After 650 CE, and in the Western Cape after 1000 CE, most San left the coasts for the interior.

When the Dutch settled at the Cape in 1652, the Cape San numbered an estimated 30,000 to 50,000. From about 1714 the Dutch East India Company’s loan farms sent Trekboer stock farmers into San lands, where they took the waterholes, shot the game and overgrazed the land. The San resisted by attacking the Boers and raiding their stock, and the Trekboers answered with commandos. From the 1770s to the late 1790s commandos surrounded camps at night and attacked at dawn, killing all the men and killing or capturing women and children; some raids killed hundreds. In 1777 the Company endorsed the eradication of the San.

Under British rule the killings fell but did not stop. By the 1850s most San had been tied to farmers by threats, the holding of wives and children, and starvation, and the Korana wars of 1868–69 and 1878–79 ended the last San of the Cape. In German South West Africa, after the governor endorsed the shooting of San, over 400 patrols went out in 1911–1913, and the San between Otavi and Gobabis fell from 8,000–12,000 in 1913 to 3,600 in 1923.
sections.legacy:
Whether the destruction of the Cape San was a genocide has been debated. Historians before the word was coined wrote of a war of extermination; N. Penn prefers “partial genocide”, and Miklós Szalay argued that the commandos chiefly sought labour, but Adhikari shows the evidence against him, above all the high ratio of San killed to those captured in 1770–1795. Official records, certainly incomplete, count 2,480 San killed and 654 captured in the last decade of Dutch East India Company rule.

In Bechuanaland the Ghanzi district was divided among white cattle farmers, making San into “farm Bushmen”. From the 1950s to the 1990s government programmes moved many San to farming. In Botswana, policies from the 1970s gave San land to majority agro-pastoralist groups and white settlers, and the government moved the residents of the Central Kalahari Game Reserve to settlements outside it, by harassment, the dismantling of services and bans on hunting, though it denies that any relocation was forced; a legal battle followed. In 2013 the United States called discrimination against the San Botswana’s “principal human rights concern”.

The San have organised to defend their rights. The Working Group of Indigenous Minorities in Southern Africa held its first general meeting in 1996, the South African San Council was founded in 2001, and in 2003 the San won a benefit-sharing agreement with South Africa’s CSIR over the hoodia plant, one of the first to pay royalties to the holders of traditional knowledge. The word San stands in the blazon of South Africa’s coat of arms.

summary: The San are the Indigenous hunter-gatherer peoples of southern Africa, descended from the region’s oldest societies and carrying some of humanity’s earliest-branching genetic lineages. Egalitarian foragers who left rock paintings across the region, they were dispossessed and killed in large numbers by colonists from the 18th century, and in Botswana and Namibia they still contend for land and recognition.

notes: Start -8000 (circa): the article’s earliest date for San societies as such is “some 10,000 years ago”, when such groups were spread from Tanzania to Cape Agulhas. Earlier dates in the article are for tools (Border Cave, 42,000 BCE, “almost identical” to modern San tools) and for genetic divergence (200,000 to 360,000–260,000 years ago); used in the text, not as the start.

Conflict inside the article: the Origins section says the San “did not have clans nor chiefs, with decisions taken by elders”, while Society says “although they had hereditary chiefs, their authority was limited”. I wrote “where there were hereditary chiefs their authority was limited” and decisions by consensus.

Genetic divergence figures differ between studies (100,000–200,000 years in the lede; 200,000/100,000 in 2016; 360,000–260,000 in 2017; isolation of 50,000–100,000 years in 2008); I gave two and said they differ.

Pre-colonial population figures conflict: the Cape San at 30,000–50,000 in the decades after 1652, against Hitchcock and Babchuk’s 300,000 San (and 600,000 Khoekhoe) in all of southern Africa in 1652. Only the first is used, as it is the Cape figure.

Mellet is named in the article without a first name or description; his claims (the Tshua and Khwe San; San involvement in founding Mapungubwe) are attributed to him. N. Penn and Adhikari are likewise given as the article gives them.

Beliefs and arts are thin in the article: no account of San cosmology, deities (the Mantis appears only in a book title), the trance dance as such, or the content of the rock art beyond its subjects. I used what is there (rainmaking trance, sacred dances, the 2006 “oldest ritual”, the eclipse belief, the Bleek collections, Lewis-Williams) and some media history to reach length. The 2006 find is described only as “the world’s oldest ritual”; the stone snake appears only in a further-reading title and is left out.

Left out: the Hoodia patent details beyond the 2003 agreement; the Equality Court ruling of 2008 on “boesman”; the novels and films list; Dave Matthews’s “most advanced people” remark (romanticising); the BBC persistence-hunt footage. The Central Kalahari eviction has no date in the article, so it is not an event. The legal battle’s outcome is not given in the article.

Pearce”, no publisher).
